conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve after having your baby.  

Today I’ll be using a short tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger.  

We’ll take it one question at a time, and if anything feels uncomfortable, just let me know—we can pause or adjust. Ready to start?  

**Question 1:** Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

(small shrug, eyes on the blanket folded in my lap)

I can still laugh… but it feels kind of forced. Like when my husband showed me that silly video of the cat knocking things off the counter, I chuckled for a second, then it just fizzled out. Most of the time nothing really strikes me as truly funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

(slow head-shake)

Not really… I mean, I’ll smile if the baby does something cute, but it’s like the laughter gets stuck. Things that used to crack me up just feel flat now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

(small sigh, fingers worrying the edge of the blanket)

I still look forward to a couple of things—like when my mom takes the baby for a walk and I can have ten quiet minutes with my coffee. But even that feels… muted. Before, I’d get excited about little plans, and now it’s more like “okay, I guess that’ll be nice.” Most stuff just feels gray.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

(eyes drop to the floor, voice softer)

Yeah… a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not reading his cues right or I’m a bad mom. I know rationally it’s not all on me, but the guilt just barges in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

(nods slowly, hugging the blanket tighter)

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly worry his breathing sounds different, or I’ll imagine him rolling off the changing table even when I’m standing right there. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just spin and I can’t snap out of them for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

(pressing my lips together, voice shaky)

A few times, yeah. Like last night, I was rocking the baby in the dark and my heart started racing—this sudden wave that something awful was about to happen. I couldn’t name what. It passed after a couple of minutes, but it left me shaky and teary.
Things have been getting on top of me

(quiet laugh, more like a huff)

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, the baby wants to be held constantly, and I think, “How is everyone else doing this?” I manage, but it’s like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

(nods, eyes rimmed red)

It’s been hard. I lie down exhausted, but my mind starts running through everything I might be messing up—did I sterilize the bottles right, is he gaining enough weight, am I already failing him? Some nights I can’t fall asleep for an hour or two, and when I do, I wake up with my heart pounding and the thoughts racing again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… most of the day, most days. It’s like there’s this heavy blanket over everything. I’ll be feeding him and tears just start leaking. I keep thinking I should feel grateful—he’s healthy, I’m physically okay—but the sadness is just there, sitting on my chest.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

(looks down, voice cracking)

A couple of times this week. Yesterday I put him in the crib for a minute, went to the bathroom, and just started sobbing over the sink. I couldn’t even say why—everything felt too big and I couldn’t stop the tears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

(swallows hard, barely above a whisper)

Once or twice… nothing I’d ever do, but the thought flickered—like, “What if I just weren’t here?” It scared me. I don’t want to leave my baby, I just want the awful feelings to stop.

You've shared that since your baby arrived laughter feels forced, most activities seem gray, and you carry a constant weight of self-blame and worry. You described <sym>intrusive anxious thoughts</sym> about your infant's safety, <sym>middle-of-the-night panic</sym>, and <sym>daily tears</sym> that come without warning. Even brief moments of respite feel muted, and, frighteningly, fleeting thoughts of escape have surfaced-though you emphasize you want help, not to leave your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh and describes a near-complete loss of enjoyment in things that previously amused them, matching the maximal severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeably reduced enjoyment and enthusiasm, describing experiences as "muted" and "gray," matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ("a lot") with persistent guilt over routine infant care, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, intrusive worries daily without cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Response conveys frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness present "most of the day, most days" with involuntary crying during routine care, matching the highest frequency option "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week with inability to stop, matching 'quite often</sym>, <sym>Response maps to "Sometimes"—patient reports fleeting passive suicidal ideation without intent.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day (Q8 score 3), markedly diminished interest (Q1 score 3), excessive guilt (Q3 score 3), insomnia (Q7 score 3), psychomotor agitation (Q4 anxiety score 3), fatigue/coping failure (Q6 score 2), recurrent tearfulness (Q9 score 2), and passive suicidal ideation (Q10 score 2). Total 25 exceeds the 14-point cutoff for urgent referral; item Q10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day review with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or local <med>perinatal mental-health crisis team</med>
2. Develop a written safety plan: list 24-hour support contacts (partner, family, National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746)
3. Consider emergency services (911 in the U.S.) if self-harm urges intensify or you fear you might act
4. Begin evidence-based treatment referral: <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> therapy plus discussion of <med>sertraline</med> or compatible antidepressant
5. Schedule daily check-ins with a trusted adult who can monitor mood, sleep, appetite, and infant care capacity
6. Enlist practical postpartum help-meals, housework, night-time bottle coverage-to protect limited sleep windows
7. Practice 5-minute paced breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic sensations</sym> arise; keep baby nearby for reassurance
8. Plan re-screen in one week to track symptom trend and treatment response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms (mother’s own words):  
- Marked anhedonia (“laughter feels flat; things feel gray”)  
- Daily pervasive sadness (“heavy blanket,” crying spells)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (“I’m a bad mom”)  
- Unwarranted anxiety & intrusive worries re infant safety  
- Discrete panic episodes (heart racing, dread, no trigger)  
- Sleep-onset and middle insomnia driven by ruminating fears  
- Sense of being overwhelmed/drowning in routine tasks  
- Passive self-harm ideation (“What if I just weren’t here?” – denies intent or plan)

Pattern: Symptoms present most of the day, most days, persisting ≥2 weeks, causing functional impairment and distress.

Risk indicators:  
☐ Persistent low mood + anhedonia  
☐ Mood-congruent insomnia  
☐ Guilt / cognitive distortions  
☐ Anxiety/panic symptoms  
☐ Feeling unable to cope  
☐ Any self-harm thought → Safety concern documented

Screening impression: High clinical likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features; passive suicidal ideation present. Recommend immediate formal psychiatric evaluation, safety planning, and support resources.
